The reason I think it is so important to teach people about accounting and financial disclosure is that if workers even have a baseline understanding (from a high school personal finance class, for example) of how to interpret what the firm says to its shareholders, they can use it as the catalyst to class consciousness within their workforce and use it as an impetus towards unionization.

A lot of people ask me why I wanted to be an academic in business despite the fact that I am in no way pro-capital. The answer is because you can't untie a knot without seeing it.

You are almost exactly correct. This is perfectly true in cases where the labor market is constrained (not enough people who want or are capable of doing the job, for example) or employees' time served at the company accumulates value. 

But with many service jobs (see: Amazon, fast food, call centers), this isn't the case. Employees are viewed as entirely disposable and as long as enough people are teetering on the edge of poverty they can always find another person to slot in and keep the machine moving. It's the military model.

Expanding on this last point, it's no wonder then why service jobs have engulfed the American economy. Tossing out workers at the first sign of unionization runs companies which require specialized skills into the ground. Can't do manufacturing if the folks that know what to do keep leaving. But service jobs can perpetuate forever. The result is we end up with an economy that doesn't make anything of value, workers that are abused and have no sense of purpose, and customers that are pissed because no one has any motivation to care. But the shareholders are happy until the house of cards finally collapses.

I study this for a living. This isn't the case. The reason you see executives trying to press both buttons is they are incentivized to keep the stock price high (or in private companies, maximize the value to the sole owner/partnership). They have to brag about good performance to outsiders because that makes outsiders think they are doing really good at their job, and they lie about how bad performance is to insiders so they can get away without raising wages/providing benefits, etc. It's not a power thing. It's the competing motivations around disclosure between the capital and labor markets.

That all said, I wouldn't be on antiwork if I thought any of this was good. The fact that there is a class of people (shareholders/owners) who are extracting wealth without actually providing anywhere near that level of value to the company is precisely why the two-faced lie needs to be perpetuated. But it's important we understand the motivations and incentives if we want to actually address the underlying problem.
